chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Khalaf ibn Hammam in a hadith of his, which he raises to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).
Regarding the Mawali (client), either he fulfills [the Imam's command] or he is divorced; if he does so, [it is accepted], but if not, his neck is struck [beheaded].
This report is Mursal (disconnected); it is not objected to with a similar [disconnected] report against the Musnad (connected) reports.

And if it were sound, it would be interpreted as referring to one who refuses to accept the ruling of the Imam, whether [refusing] divorce or fulfillment, in opposition to him and to the Sharia of Islam.
For whoever has this description is considered a disbeliever, and killing him is obligatory upon him.

As for one who is not like that, it is not obligatory upon him to be killed; rather, imprisonment and constriction upon him until he is divorced or fulfills [the obligation] is sufficient, according to what the first two reports contained.

key_terms.الْإِمَامِ: The Imam, referring to the divinely appointed leader whose rulings are binding.
key_terms.الْقَتْلُ: Killing/Execution, here specified as the penalty for obstinate refusal.
key_terms.الْمُوَلَّى: Mawali (client/dependent), a specific social-legal category in Shia jurisprudence.
key_terms.مُرْسَلٌ: Mursal (disconnected), a type of hadith where a tabi'i narrates directly from the Prophet or Imam without a companion in the chain.
key_terms.مُسَنَدٌ: Musnad (connected), a hadith with a continuous chain of narrators back to the source.
key_terms.يُوفِيَ: To fulfill or pay (often referring to a financial or conditional obligation).

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling for a Mawali who refuses the Imam's command to divorce or fulfill an obligation?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that the severe penalty of beheading for the 'Mawali' applies specifically to those who obstinately reject the Imam's authority, rendering them apostates, while ordinary non-compliance warrants imprisonment and pressure. This distinction highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of differentiating between simple disobedience and defiant rejection of divine law, ensuring that the harsher punishment is not applied universally. The report is classified as Mursal but is considered authoritative enough to stand against other narrations due to its clear contextual application.
